period.note: died in Rome, according to tradition, between 64 and early 68; exact year unknown

facts.text: Peter, also called Simon or Cephas, was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee and one of the Twelve; the Gospels list him first.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles

facts.text: Catholic tradition holds that he led the Church in Rome and was martyred there under Nero.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles

facts.text: His exact death year is not recorded in Scripture; the Catholic Encyclopedia places it between July 64 and the beginning of 68.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles

period.note: died in Rome under Nero, according to tradition; year uncertain (c. 64-68)

facts.text: Paul of Tarsus came from a family attached to Pharisaic tradition and persecuted the Church until his conversion, which Acts narrates on the road to Damascus.
He travelled widely as a missionary to the Gentiles, and letters bearing his name make up a large part of the New Testament.
Tradition holds that he was beheaded in Rome under Nero; the exact year is uncertain.
Andrew was a fisherman, the brother of Simon Peter, and one of the Twelve; the Gospel of John says he first followed John the Baptist.
Tradition says he was martyred at Patras in Achaia; the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the X-shaped cross associated with him is attested only from about the fourteenth century.
John was a fisherman, brother of James, and one of the Twelve; the Gospels name him among Jesus' closest disciples.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. John the Evangelist

facts.text: Tradition identifies him as the author of the Fourth Gospel, three letters and Revelation, though scholars debate each attribution.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. John the Evangelist

facts.text: Ancient tradition places his later life and death at Ephesus.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. John the Evangelist

facts.text: Stephen was one of the seven men chosen to serve the Greek-speaking widows of the Jerusalem community.
He was stoned outside the city after speaking to the council; the Church honours him as the first Christian martyr.

period.note: martyred at Rome under Trajan; c. 107 is the traditional date, the Catholic Encyclopedia says between 98 and 117

facts.text: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch and was taken in chains to Rome to be killed for his faith.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Ignatius of Antioch

facts.text: On the journey he wrote seven letters, six to churches and one to Polycarp, which survive.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Ignatius of Antioch

facts.text: His martyrdom at Rome is placed under Trajan (reigned 98-117); the Catholic Encyclopedia gives no single year and some scholars date it later.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Ignatius of Antioch

period.note: martyred c. 155; some scholars propose a date in the 160s

facts.text: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna; his letter to the Philippians survives.
The Catholic Encyclopedia gives February 155 as the probable date of his martyrdom, on 23 February; it names 166 as the other possible year.
Irenaeus recalled hearing him as a boy.
Justin was born at Flavia Neapolis in Palestine, was educated in philosophy, became a Christian, and defended the faith in works such as the First Apology.
He was martyred at Rome about AD 165, after being condemned by the prefect Rusticus.
Irenaeus was a priest and then bishop of Lyons, succeeding the martyred Pothinus.
As a young man he had heard Polycarp, which links him to the apostolic generation.
His date of death is unknown; it fell at the end of the second or the start of the third century.
Cyprian became bishop of Carthage around 248 or the beginning of 249, soon after he converted.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Cyprian of Carthage

facts.text: He led his church through the Decian persecution and argued with Rome over the rebaptism of heretics.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Cyprian of Carthage

facts.text: He was beheaded at Carthage in 258.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Cyprian of Carthage

facts.text: Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria in 328 and defended the full divinity of the Son against Arianism.
He was exiled several times for his stand.
The Life of Antony is traditionally attributed to him.
He died on 2 May 373.
Basil was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from 370 and a major defender of Nicene faith.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Basil the Great

facts.text: He is credited with monastic Rules that became influential in Eastern monasticism.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Basil the Great

facts.text: He died on 1 January 379; his birth is usually placed about 329.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Basil the Great

period.note: born c. 325 (Catholic Encyclopedia), some place it c. 329-330; died 389 or 390

facts.text: Gregory was a friend of Basil and one of the three Cappadocian Fathers.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Gregory of Nazianzus

facts.text: He is known as 'the Theologian' for his orations on the Trinity, and he led the Nicene community in Constantinople from 379.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Gregory of Nazianzus

facts.text: He died about 389 or 390 at his family estate at Arianzus; his birth year is uncertain.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Gregory of Nazianzus

facts.text: John was a priest of Antioch whose preaching earned him the title Chrysostom, 'golden mouth'.
He became archbishop of Constantinople in 398 and was driven into exile after clashing with the court.
He died on 14 September 407 while being taken to a remote place of exile; his birth is placed around 347.
Ambrose was a Roman governor of Liguria and Aemilia who was chosen bishop of Milan by acclamation while still a catechumen.
He defended Nicene faith against Arians, and his preaching helped bring Augustine to the faith; he baptized Augustine at Milan about Easter 387.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Augustine of Hippo

facts.text: He died on 4 April 397; his birth year is given as about 340.

period.note: born in the 340s, exact year uncertain

facts.text: Jerome was a scholar who translated the Bible into Latin; his version became the basis of the Vulgate.
He spent his later years in Bethlehem, where he wrote commentaries and letters, and he died there in 420.
His birth year is uncertain and falls somewhere in the 340s.
Augustine was born in 354 at Thagaste in North Africa and was baptized by Ambrose in Milan in 387.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Augustine of Hippo

facts.text: He became bishop of Hippo and wrote the Confessions and the City of God.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Augustine of Hippo

facts.text: He died in 430 while Hippo was under siege by the Vandals.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Augustine of Hippo

facts.text: Gregory was a Roman official who became a monk and was elected pope in 590.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Gregory the Great

facts.text: He sent monks to convert the Anglo-Saxons and wrote the Pastoral Rule and the Dialogues.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Gregory the Great

facts.text: He died in 604; his birth is placed around 540.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Gregory the Great

facts.text: Leo was consecrated bishop of Rome on 29 September 440 and governed the Roman Church for about twenty-one years.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), Pope St. Leo I (The Great)

facts.text: His letter to Flavian, known as the Tome, shaped the Christological definition at Chalcedon in 451.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), Pope St. Leo I (The Great)

facts.text: He died in 461.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), Pope St. Leo I (The Great)

facts.text: Benedict was born at Nursia in Italy, lived as a hermit at Subiaco, and later founded the monastery of Monte Cassino.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Benedict of Nursia

facts.text: He wrote the Rule of St. Benedict, the most influential rule for Western monks.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Benedict of Nursia

facts.text: His dates are traditional: born about 480, died about 543 according to the Catholic Encyclopedia (some place his death a few years later).

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Benedict of Nursia

facts.text: Bede was an English monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow who wrote biblical commentaries and the Ecclesiastical History of the English People.
He died in 735, on the vigil of the Ascension.
Anselm was born in Aosta, became a monk and abbot at Bec, and in 1093 was made archbishop of Canterbury.
He wrote the Proslogion and Cur Deus Homo, and he died on 21 April 1109.
Bernard became a Cistercian monk and in 1115 was made first abbot of Clairvaux.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Bernard of Clairvaux

facts.text: He was an influential preacher and adviser to popes and kings, and he wrote sermons on the Song of Songs.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Bernard of Clairvaux

facts.text: He died in 1153; his birth is given as 1090 or 1091.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Bernard of Clairvaux

facts.text: Francis was born in Assisi in about 1181 or 1182, gave up his family's wealth, and founded the Franciscan Order.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Francis of Assisi

facts.text: He died at Assisi on 3 October 1226 and was canonized by Gregory IX in 1228.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Francis of Assisi

facts.text: Dominic was born at Calaruega in Castile around 1170 and founded the Order of Preachers.
The order was approved by Honorius III in December 1216.
He died at Bologna on 6 August 1221.
Anthony was born in Lisbon in 1195, left the Augustinian canons, and joined the Franciscans.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Anthony of Padua

facts.text: He was a noted preacher and died near Padua on 13 June 1231; Gregory IX canonized him in 1232.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Anthony of Padua

facts.text: Thomas was a Dominican friar and theologian who taught at Paris and in Italy.
His chief work is the Summa Theologiae; he left it unfinished.
He died on 7 March 1274 at Fossanova on his way to the Council of Lyons; his birth is dated about 1225.
Bonaventure was a Franciscan theologian who taught at Paris and became Minister General of his order in 1257.
He was made cardinal-bishop of Albano and died at the Council of Lyons in 1274.

period.note: born between about 1193 and 1206; exact year unknown

facts.text: Albert was a German Dominican who taught at Paris and Cologne and wrote on theology and natural science.
Thomas Aquinas was among his students.
He died at Cologne in 1280; his birth year is uncertain (c. 1206 in the Catholic Encyclopedia, 1193 in some other accounts).
Catherine was a Dominican tertiary from Siena who worked to bring peace among Italian cities.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Catherine of Siena

facts.text: She urged Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome and wrote letters and the Dialogue.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Catherine of Siena

facts.text: She died in Rome on 29 April 1380.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Catherine of Siena

facts.text: Teresa was born at Avila in 1515, became a Carmelite, and led a reform of her order that produced the Discalced Carmelites.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Teresa of Jesus (Teresa of Avila)

facts.text: She wrote her Life and the Interior Castle, and she died in 1582.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Teresa of Jesus (Teresa of Avila)

facts.text: She was canonized in 1622.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Teresa of Jesus (Teresa of Avila)

facts.text: John was born in Old Castile in 1542 and helped Teresa begin the Discalced reform among Carmelite friars.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. John of the Cross

facts.text: He was imprisoned in Toledo in December 1577 and escaped in August 1578.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. John of the Cross

facts.text: He wrote The Ascent of Mount Carmel and The Dark Night, and died at Ubeda on 14 December 1591.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. John of the Cross

facts.text: Ignatius was born in 1491 at the castle of Loyola in Spain and was a soldier before his conversion.
At Manresa he began the notes that became the Spiritual Exercises.
He founded the Society of Jesus, approved in 1540, and died at Rome on 31 July 1556.
Francis de Sales was bishop of Geneva, living at Annecy, and a leading preacher of the Catholic reform.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Francis de Sales

facts.text: He wrote the Introduction to the Devout Life and co-founded the Visitation Order with Jane de Chantal.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Francis de Sales

facts.text: He died at Lyons on 28 December 1622.

source.label: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), St. Francis de Sales

facts.text: Alphonsus was a lawyer from Naples who became a priest and founded the Redemptorists in 1732.
He wrote widely on moral theology and prayer, and he died in 1787.
Therese Martin entered the Carmel of Lisieux at the age of fifteen, in 1888, and her autobiographical manuscripts were published as Story of a Soul.

source.label: John Paul II, Divini Amoris Scientia (1997), vatican.va

facts.text: John Paul II declared her a Doctor of the Church on 19 October 1997.

source.label: John Paul II, Divini Amoris Scientia (1997), vatican.va

facts.text: She died on 30 September 1897, aged 24.

source.label: John Paul II, Divini Amoris Scientia (1997), vatican.va

facts.text: Thomas More was an English lawyer, writer and Lord Chancellor who refused to accept Henry VIII's supremacy over the Church.
He was executed on 6 July 1535.
He was beatified in 1886 and canonized by Pius XI in 1935.
Perpetua was a young noblewoman of Carthage who was arrested as a catechumen with her slave Felicity.
She and her companions were killed in the arena in 203; part of the account of her imprisonment is attributed to her own diary.
Maximilian Kolbe was a Polish Conventual Franciscan who founded the Niepokalanow publishing centre.

source.label: Vatican biography of Maximilian Maria Kolbe (canonization, 10 Oct 1982)

facts.text: He was arrested by the Gestapo in 1941, sent to Auschwitz, and offered to die in place of another prisoner.

source.label: Vatican biography of Maximilian Maria Kolbe (canonization, 10 Oct 1982)

facts.text: He died on 14 August 1941; John Paul II canonized him on 10 October 1982.

source.label: Vatican biography of Maximilian Maria Kolbe (canonization, 10 Oct 1982)

facts.text: Karol Wojtyla was born at Wadowice, Poland, on 18 May 1920.

source.label: Vatican, biographical profile of John Paul II

facts.text: He was elected pope on 16 October 1978 and died on 2 April 2005.

source.label: Vatican, biographical profile of John Paul II

facts.text: Benedict XVI beatified him on 1 May 2011.

source.label: Vatican, biographical profile of John Paul II

facts.text: Francis canonized him, together with John XXIII, on 27 April 2014.

source.label: Francis, homily at the canonization of John XXIII and John Paul II, 27 April 2014, vatican.va

facts.text: God formed the first man from the dust of the ground, breathed life into him, and placed him in a garden in Eden.
Adam ate the fruit God had forbidden, and he was then sent out of the garden.
Adam and Eve were the parents of Cain, Abel and Seth.
Genesis records that Adam lived 930 years and then died.
God made the first woman from one of the man’s ribs and brought her to the man.
Adam named his wife Eve because she was to be the mother of all the living.
Eve bore Cain, and later Seth, whom she saw as a replacement for Abel.
Noah found favour with God and is described as a righteous man who walked with God.
God told Noah to build an ark to save his family and pairs of every kind of animal from a coming flood.
After the flood God made a covenant with Noah and every living creature, with the rainbow as its sign.
Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth, and lived 950 years.
God called Abram to leave his homeland for a land he would be shown, with a promise of blessing for all the families of the earth.
In a covenant with God, Abram’s name was changed to Abraham, meaning father of many nations.
Isaac was born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age, as God had promised.
God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac; an angel stopped him, and God provided a ram instead.
Sarai was the wife of Abram. Genesis 20:12 adds that she was also his half-sister.
God changed her name from Sarai to Sarah and promised that she would bear a son.
Sarah bore Isaac when she was old, as promised.
Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (Hebron), and Abraham buried her in the cave of Machpelah that he bought.
Isaac was the son promised to Abraham and Sarah.
Isaac was the son Abraham was told to offer, and was spared when God provided a ram.
Isaac married Rebekah and was comforted after his mother’s death.
Isaac was the father of the twins Esau and Jacob.
Rebekah, a relative of Abraham, drew water at a well and offered it to Abraham’s servant and his camels.
She agreed to leave her family and go with the servant to marry Isaac.
Rebekah gave birth to twin sons, Esau and Jacob.
She helped Jacob to receive the blessing of Isaac in place of Esau.
Jacob was the younger of Isaac’s twin sons and was born gripping his brother Esau’s heel.
At Bethel Jacob dreamed of a stairway between earth and heaven, and God renewed the promise to him.
After wrestling through the night, Jacob was given the new name Israel.
Jacob had twelve sons, listed in Genesis 35:22-26, and he died and was gathered to his people.
Joseph was born to Jacob and Rachel; she named him Joseph.
His brothers sold him to traders who took him to Egypt.
Pharaoh put Joseph in charge of Egypt after he interpreted Pharaoh’s dreams.
Joseph told his brothers that God had sent him ahead of them to preserve life during the famine.
Moses was born to a Levite family, hidden in a basket by the Nile, and raised by Pharaoh’s daughter.
God spoke to Moses from a burning bush and sent him to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
At Mount Sinai Moses received the Ten Commandments for the people.
At Mount Sinai God spoke the Ten Commandments to the people and gave Moses the two stone tablets of the covenant.
Aaron was Moses’ brother, and God said he would speak for Moses to the people.
God chose Aaron and his sons to serve as priests, and they were consecrated.
Aaron made a golden calf when the people grew impatient while Moses was on the mountain.
Aaron died on Mount Hor, and his son Eleazar took his priestly garments.
Miriam was a sister of Moses and Aaron, children of Amram and Jochebed.
Miriam is called a prophetess; she led the women with tambourines in song after the crossing of the sea.
She spoke against Moses, was struck with a skin disease, and was healed after Moses prayed.
The unnamed sister who watched over the baby Moses is traditionally taken to be Miriam, but the text does not name her.
Hoshea son of Nun was renamed Joshua by Moses.
Moses laid his hands on Joshua at God’s command and commissioned him as leader.
Joshua led Israel in the capture of Jericho.
Joshua urged the people to serve the Lord, saying he and his household would do so, and he died aged 110.
Ruth was a Moabite woman who stayed with her mother-in-law Naomi and pledged to follow her people and her God.
She gathered grain in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi’s late husband.
Ruth married Boaz and bore Obed, who became the grandfather of David.
Matthew lists Ruth in the ancestry of Jesus.
Samuel was born to Hannah after she prayed for a child.
As a boy ministering to the Lord before Eli, he heard the Lord call his name and answered.
Samuel anointed Saul, telling him the Lord sent him to anoint him king over Israel, and later anointed David.
Samuel died, and all Israel mourned him.
David was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, and Samuel anointed him in the presence of his brothers.
David defeated the Philistine Goliath with a sling and a stone.
Through the prophet Nathan, God promised that David’s house and throne would endure.
David sinned against Uriah and Bathsheba, was rebuked by Nathan, and admitted, “I have sinned against the Lord.”
Solomon was a son of David and Bathsheba.
David had Solomon anointed king at Gihon.
At Gibeon Solomon asked God for an understanding heart, and God granted him wisdom.
Solomon built the temple for the Lord, but in later life his foreign wives turned his heart toward other gods.
Elijah the Tishbite, from Gilead, told King Ahab that there would be no rain except at his word.
On Mount Carmel Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal, and fire from the Lord consumed his sacrifice.
Elijah was taken up into heaven in a whirlwind.
Malachi says Elijah will be sent before the day of the Lord, and Elijah appears with Moses at the Transfiguration.
Elijah called Elisha, son of Shaphat, by throwing his cloak over him while he was ploughing.
After Elijah was taken up, Elisha took up his cloak and the prophets recognised that Elijah’s spirit rested on him.
Elisha restored to life the son of the woman of Shunem.
He told the Syrian commander Naaman to wash in the Jordan, and Naaman was healed.
Isaiah was the son of Amoz and received his visions in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.
In a vision in the temple he saw the Lord enthroned, was cleansed, and answered, “Here I am, send me.”
He gave King Ahaz a sign: a virgin would conceive and bear a son called Immanuel.
King Hezekiah sent messengers to Isaiah when Jerusalem was threatened, and Isaiah gave him a message of reassurance.
Jeremiah was a priest’s son from Anathoth whom God called as a prophet while he was still young.
The priest Pashhur had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks.
Jeremiah dictated his messages to the scribe Baruch, who wrote them on a scroll.
Officials threw Jeremiah into a cistern, and Ebed-melech had him pulled out.
Ezekiel was a priest, the son of Buzi, among the exiles by the Chebar canal in Babylonia when he saw visions of God.
God sent him to the rebellious people of Israel and had him eat a scroll of words.
God made Ezekiel a watchman responsible for warning the people.
In a vision of dry bones that came to life, he was told God would restore Israel.
Daniel was one of the young Judeans taken to Babylon and trained for the king’s service.
He interpreted Nebuchadnezzar’s dream and was given a high position in Babylon.
Daniel was thrown into a den of lions for praying to his God, and he was kept safe.
Esther was a Jewish orphan raised by her relative Mordecai.
The king of Persia loved her and made her queen in place of Vashti.
Mordecai urged her to speak for her people; she asked the Jews of Susa to fast for her three days and said she would then go in to the king.
She told the king of Haman’s plot against the Jews and named Haman as the enemy.
Judith was a wealthy and devout widow of Bethulia who lived by prayer and fasting.
She struck off the head of Holofernes as he lay in his tent.
Ozias (Uzziah) blessed her above all the women of the earth for what she had done.
Some readers treat the book of Judith as history and others as a religious story with a teaching purpose.
Tobit was of the tribe of Naphtali and was carried off into captivity by the Assyrians.
He gave alms and buried the dead who had been left unburied.
He became blind when bird droppings fell into his eyes as he slept.
His sight was restored when his son rubbed medicine on his eyes, and the companion Raphael later revealed himself as one of the seven holy angels.
Job lived in the land of Uz and is described as blameless, upright and God-fearing.
He lost his children and property in one day and said, “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”
God answered Job out of the whirlwind, and afterward restored his fortunes.
James holds up Job as an example of patient endurance.
The angel Gabriel announced to Mary of Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, that she would bear a son; she answered, “Let it be done to me according to your word.”
Mary gave birth to her firstborn son in Bethlehem.
Mary stood by the cross, and Jesus entrusted her to the disciple whom he loved.
Later tradition names Mary’s parents as Joachim and Anne. Scripture does not name them.
Joseph, a righteous man betrothed to Mary, was told in a dream to take her as his wife and name her child Jesus.
Warned in dreams, Joseph took Mary and Jesus to Egypt and later settled in Nazareth.
The people of Nazareth called Jesus “the carpenter’s son,” which suggests Joseph worked as a craftsman.
Joseph and Mary took Jesus to Jerusalem for the Passover when he was twelve.
John was born to the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, and was named John as the angel had said.
He preached a baptism of repentance in the wilderness and the region around the Jordan.
John pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, and two of his disciples followed Jesus.
Herod had John imprisoned and later had him beheaded.

profiles.name: Elizabeth, mother of John the Baptist

facts.text: Elizabeth was the wife of the priest Zechariah and was herself of Aaron’s line; they were childless.
The angel told Mary that her relative Elizabeth was expecting a child in her old age.
When Mary greeted her, the child leapt in Elizabeth’s womb and she called Mary the mother of her Lord.
Elizabeth gave birth and insisted that the child be named John.
Andrew brought his brother Simon to Jesus, who gave him the name Cephas, meaning Peter.
Simon declared Jesus to be the Christ, and Jesus called him Peter and promised to build his church on this rock.
Peter denied Jesus three times, and after the resurrection Jesus asked him three times, “Do you love me?” and told him to feed his sheep.
Early Christian writers record that Peter and Paul were martyred at Rome. Scripture does not report it.
Andrew was one of two disciples of John the Baptist who followed Jesus after John pointed him out.
Andrew was a fisherman who left his nets to follow Jesus with his brother Simon.
Andrew pointed out the boy with five loaves and two fish before the feeding of the crowd.
Philip told Andrew about some Greeks who wished to see Jesus, and the two went to Jesus together.
James and his brother John left their father Zebedee and their boat when Jesus called them.
Jesus gave James and John the name Boanerges, meaning sons of thunder.
James was with Peter and John on the mountain at the Transfiguration.
King Herod had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.
John, son of Zebedee, was called by Jesus with his brother James and followed him.
John went with Peter to the temple, and the two healed a man lame from birth.
Church tradition identifies the “disciple whom Jesus loved” of John 13:23 and 21:20-24 with John the apostle. The Gospel of John does not name him.
The book of Revelation names its author as John, who was on the island of Patmos.
Whether the John of Revelation is the apostle is debated.
Jesus called Matthew as he sat at the tax collector’s booth, and Matthew got up and followed him.
Mark and Luke tell the same story of a tax collector named Levi, which is generally taken to be the same man.
Matthew the tax collector is named among the twelve apostles.
Early tradition credits Matthew with the first Gospel. The Gospel itself carries no author’s name.
Thomas, called Didymus, urged the other disciples to go with Jesus, saying they might die with him.
Thomas asked Jesus how they could know the way when they did not know where he was going.
Thomas was absent when Jesus first appeared; a week later he saw the risen Jesus and said, “My Lord and my God!”
Tradition, recorded by Eusebius, says Thomas was allotted Parthia as his mission field. Scripture does not report this.
Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, travelled with Jesus and supported him.
Mary Magdalene stood near the cross with the other women.
She saw the risen Jesus at the tomb and was sent to tell his disciples.
Scripture does not say she is the sinful woman of Luke 7 or Mary of Bethany; Gregory the Great combined them in a sixth-century homily, and this is not a settled identification.

source.label: Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels 33

facts.text: Martha welcomed Jesus into her home and was busy serving, while her sister Mary sat listening at his feet.
Martha and her sister Mary lived at Bethany, and Jesus loved Martha, Mary and their brother Lazarus.
When Lazarus died, Martha told Jesus, “I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God.”
At a supper in Bethany Martha served.
Lazarus of Bethany was the brother of Martha and Mary, and Jesus loved him.
Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb four days after his death.
Crowds came to see Lazarus, and the chief priests planned to kill him as well.
Scripture does not identify the Lazarus of Bethany with the beggar named Lazarus in Jesus’ parable.
Paul was a Jew born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem, a Pharisee of the tribe of Benjamin, and trained under Gamaliel.
Saul, who had been persecuting Christians, met the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and was baptised.
He was sent out from Antioch with Barnabas, and in Acts he is called Paul from the time of the mission in Cyprus.
Early Christian writers record that Paul was martyred at Rome. Scripture does not report it.
A Levite from Cyprus, called Joses (Joseph in the Douay-Rheims) and named Barnabas by the apostles, he sold a field and gave the money to the apostles.
Barnabas brought Saul to the apostles in Jerusalem and vouched for him.
He was sent to Antioch and then fetched Saul from Tarsus to work with him there.
Barnabas parted from Paul over whether to take John Mark on a journey.
Timothy was a disciple from Lystra whose mother was a Jewish believer and whose father was Greek; Paul took him as a companion.
Paul recalls the faith that lived first in Timothy’s grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice.
Paul calls Timothy his true child in the faith.
Paul sent Timothy to strengthen the church in Thessalonica.
Stephen was one of seven men chosen to serve at the daily distribution to widows, and is described as full of faith and the Holy Spirit.
He worked wonders among the people and was accused before the council.
He was stoned outside the city, and as he died he prayed that the Lord not hold the sin against his killers.
Devout men buried Stephen and mourned for him.
Paul sends greetings from “Luke the beloved physician.”
Paul wrote that only Luke was with him.
Early tradition names Luke, a follower of Paul, as the author of the third Gospel and of Acts. Neither book names its author.
From this point the narrative of Acts sometimes shifts to “we,” which suggests the writer was travelling with Paul.

identification.modern: Jerusalem, on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains (the Old City and the City of David ridge); the city's political status is disputed

facts.text: David captured the stronghold of Zion and named it the City of David.
The infant Jesus was brought to the Temple here, where Simeon and Anna recognised him.
The emperor Hadrian refounded Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were forbidden to enter it.

identification.modern: Bethlehem, in the Judaean Mountains about 10 km south of Jerusalem, West Bank

facts.text: Matthew places the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod.
The prophet Micah names Bethlehem Ephrathah as the town from which a ruler of Israel would come.
Ruth's husband's family came from Bethlehem of Judah.

identification.modern: Nazareth, in Lower Galilee, Northern District, Israel

facts.text: The angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin named Mary in Nazareth, a town of Galilee.
Jesus grew up in Nazareth and taught in its synagogue on the Sabbath.
Nathanael asks, 'Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?'

identification.modern: Tell Hum, on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, Israel

source.label: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Archaeology in Israel: Capernaum'

facts.text: Matthew says Jesus left Nazareth and made his home in Capernaum by the sea.
Jesus entered the synagogue at Capernaum and taught, and then healed Peter's mother-in-law and many others at the house of Simon and Andrew.

Franciscan excavations, renewed between 1968 and 1972, uncovered a house that Christian tradition identifies as the house of Peter; an octagonal church was built over the earlier remains in the mid fifth century.

source.label: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Archaeology in Israel: Capernaum'

identification.modern: Al-Eizariya, on the southeastern slope of the Mount of Olives, less than 2 miles (3.2 km) from Jerusalem, West Bank

facts.text: Bethany was the village of Mary, Martha and their brother Lazarus.
It lay about fifteen stadia (roughly three kilometres) from Jerusalem.
John also mentions a different Bethany, beyond the Jordan, where John the Baptist was baptizing.

identification.modern: Tell es-Sultan (ancient Jericho) and the modern city of Jericho in the Jordan Valley, West Bank

facts.text: Joshua 6 tells how the Israelites marched around Jericho and its wall fell.
In the parable of the Good Samaritan the traveller goes down from Jerusalem to Jericho.
Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, lived in Jericho and welcomed Jesus into his house.

identification.modern: Disputed. Candidates include Kafr Kanna and Khirbet Qana in Galilee, Israel; other sites have also been proposed

facts.text: John places the first sign of Jesus, the water changed into wine at a wedding, at Cana in Galilee.
Jesus, at Cana, healed the son of a royal official who lay sick at Capernaum.
The location of Cana is disputed. A tradition dating from the 8th century identifies it with the town of Kafr Kanna, and Khirbet Qana has also long been proposed.

identification.modern: Banias, at the foot of Mount Hermon, in the Golan Heights

facts.text: Jesus asked his disciples who people say he is in the region of Caesarea Philippi.
In that region Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus spoke of building his Church on the rock.

identification.modern: Lake Kinneret (Sea of Galilee), in northeast Israel between the Golan Heights and Galilee

facts.text: Luke calls it the Lake of Gennesaret, and John calls it the Sea of Tiberias.
Jesus called Simon, Andrew, James and John, who were fishermen, beside this sea.
Jesus calmed a storm on the lake and walked on its water.

identification.modern: The Jordan River, flowing from the Mount Hermon headwaters through the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, along the borders of Israel, Jordan, the West Bank and the Golan Heights

facts.text: Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground under Joshua.
Naaman the Syrian was cleansed after washing seven times in the Jordan.
Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John.

identification.modern: Disputed. Jebel Musa in the south-central Sinai Peninsula (Egypt), above St Catherine's Monastery, was a major contender by the 4th century; Jebel Serbal, also in southern Sinai, is another proposal

source.label: Biblical Archaeology Society, 'The Case for (or Against) Jebel Musa'

facts.text: Exodus says the LORD came down on Mount Sinai and gave the law to Moses there.
Exodus calls Horeb 'God's mountain', and Deuteronomy says the LORD made a covenant with Israel at Horeb.
The mountain's location is uncertain: Jebel Musa was a major contender by the 4th century, and Jebel Serbal, also in southern Sinai, is another proposal.

source.label: Biblical Archaeology Society, 'The Case for (or Against) Jebel Musa'

identification.modern: Mount of Olives, a ridge in East Jerusalem, east of the Old City across the Kidron Valley

facts.text: Jesus went to the Mount of Olives as was his custom, and prayed there before his arrest.
Acts places the Ascension near Jerusalem and says Olivet was a Sabbath day's journey from the city.
Zechariah foretells that the LORD will stand on the Mount of Olives east of Jerusalem.

identification.modern: Disputed. The name first belonged to the Jebusite city on the Eastern Hill (City of David) and later shifted; today Mount Zion is the Western Hill just outside the Old City walls to the south

facts.text: David captured the stronghold of Zion and called it the City of David.
In early Christian times 'Sion' came to be used as another name for Jerusalem, and the name Sion was applied to the Cenacle, the traditional Upper Room.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of Mount Zion as the heavenly Jerusalem that believers have approached.

identification.modern: Hebron (Al-Khalil), in the southern West Bank about 30 km south of Jerusalem

facts.text: Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron as a burial place for Sarah.
David was anointed king over Judah at Hebron.
David reigned at Hebron for seven years and six months before ruling from Jerusalem.

identification.modern: Probably Beitin, about 5 km northeast of Ramallah, West Bank

facts.text: After his dream of the ladder, Jacob named the place Bethel; its earlier name was Luz.
King Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan.

identification.modern: Tell Balata, east of the modern city of Nablus, West Bank

facts.text: Abram came to Shechem, to the oak of Moreh, where the LORD promised the land to his descendants.
Joshua gathered the tribes at Shechem and renewed the covenant.

Genesis says Jacob bought a parcel of ground at Shechem, and Joshua says Joseph's bones were buried there; John places Jesus' meeting with the Samaritan woman at Sychar, near the plot Jacob gave to Joseph.
Scholars do not agree whether John's Sychar is Shechem itself or a nearby village.

identification.modern: Sebastia, a village near Nablus, West Bank

facts.text: King Omri bought the hill of Samaria and built a city there as the capital of the northern kingdom.
The king of Assyria besieged and captured Samaria and deported Israelites.
Philip proclaimed the Christ in the city of Samaria, and there was great joy in that city.

identification.modern: Damascus, Syria

facts.text: Saul was struck by a light from heaven near Damascus and was later baptized there.
Ananias was sent to a house on the street called Straight.
Paul escaped from Damascus by being let down the wall in a basket.

identification.modern: Antakya, Hatay Province, Turkey (the ancient city lies under the modern town)

facts.text: The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.
The church at Antioch sent Barnabas and Saul out on the first missionary journey.
Paul confronted Peter at Antioch over eating with Gentile believers.

identification.modern: Ruins near present-day Selçuk, İzmir Province, Turkey

facts.text: Paul taught at Ephesus for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord.
A riot led by the silversmiths broke out over the cult of Artemis (Diana) of the Ephesians.
The third ecumenical council, held at Ephesus in 431, excluded Nestorius from episcopal office.

identification.modern: Ancient Corinth, on the Isthmus of Corinth in the Peloponnese region, Greece (the modern city lies about 5 km to the northeast)

facts.text: Paul stayed in Corinth a year and six months, teaching the word of God.
He wrote two letters to the church of God that is at Corinth.
Paul met Aquila and Priscilla at Corinth.

identification.modern: Ruins near the village of Filippoi, within the municipality of Kavala, East Macedonia and Thrace, Greece

facts.text: Luke calls Philippi a leading city of Macedonia and a Roman colony.
Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, was baptized there with her household.
Paul wrote the Letter to the Philippians to the saints in Philippi, with their overseers and deacons.

identification.modern: Thessaloniki, on the Thermaic Gulf, Greece

facts.text: Paul reasoned in the synagogue at Thessalonica on three Sabbaths.
He wrote two letters to the church of the Thessalonians.
The Philippians sent aid to Paul more than once while he was in Thessalonica.

identification.modern: Rome, Italy

facts.text: Paul wrote his letter to all God's beloved in Rome.
Paul lived under guard in Rome for two years in his own rented lodging and preached openly.
The Lord told Paul that he must bear witness in Rome as he had in Jerusalem.

identification.modern: Athens, Greece

facts.text: Paul was troubled to see the city full of idols and spoke in the marketplace.
He addressed the Areopagus and referred to an altar inscribed 'To an unknown god'.
Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris were among those who believed.

identification.modern: Central Anatolia, Turkey (roughly the provinces of Ankara and Eskişehir). Scholars debate whether Paul's 'Galatians' lived in the northern ethnic region or the southern Roman province

facts.text: Paul addresses his letter to the churches of Galatia.
Luke says Paul and his companions passed through the region of Phrygia and Galatia.

Scholars disagree whether the Letter to the Galatians was addressed to churches in the north of the region (North Galatian view) or to churches Paul founded in the southern part of the Roman province (South Galatian view).

identification.modern: Tarsus, Mersin Province, Turkey, about 20 km inland from the Mediterranean

facts.text: Paul called himself a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city.
The believers sent Saul to Tarsus after the plot against him in Jerusalem.
Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul and brought him to Antioch.

identification.modern: Disputed. Candidates near Jerusalem include Emmaus-Nicopolis (Imwas), Abu Ghosh, al-Qubeibeh and Motza

facts.text: On Easter day two disciples walking to Emmaus, one named Cleopas, met the risen Jesus and knew him in the breaking of the bread.
Most manuscripts of Luke give the distance from Jerusalem as sixty stadia, but several manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus, give 160.
The sixty-stadia reading fits Abu Ghosh or al-Qubeibeh, while the 160-stadia reading fits Emmaus-Nicopolis, long identified as Emmaus since the 4th century. The site is not settled.

identification.modern: Tell el-Muqayyar, Dhi Qar Governorate, southern Iraq, is the usual identification; other sites have been proposed

facts.text: Terah took his son Abram from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to Canaan, and they settled in Haran.
God told Abram that he had brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans.
Tell el-Muqayyar was recognised as Ur when Henry Rawlinson deciphered inscribed bricks from the site, and Leonard Woolley led excavations there from 1922 to 1934.

identification.modern: Probably Harran, Şanlıurfa Province, southeastern Turkey, about 40 km southeast of Urfa

facts.text: Terah died in Haran after the family settled there.
Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran at the LORD's command.
On his journey to Haran Jacob met shepherds who said they were from Haran and who knew Laban.

identification.modern: Ruins across the Tigris from the historic centre of Mosul, Iraq, with the mounds Tell Kuyunjiq and Tell Nabi Yunus

facts.text: God sent Jonah to Nineveh, the great city, to preach against its wickedness.
The people of Nineveh believed God and proclaimed a fast after Jonah's preaching.
After the disaster to his army, Sennacherib of Assyria departed, went home and lived at Nineveh.

identification.modern: Ruins near Hillah, Babil Governorate, Iraq, on the lower Euphrates about 85 km south of Baghdad

facts.text: Genesis says the place of the tower was named Babel because the LORD confused the language of all the earth there.
The Hebrew Bible uses the name Babel for the city of Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar carried the leaders and craftsmen of Jerusalem into exile in Babylon.
The exiles wept by the rivers of Babylon when they remembered Zion.

identification.modern: Probably the eastern Nile Delta, Egypt; the western Wadi Tumilat is a leading proposal and scholars disagree on the exact area

facts.text: Joseph invited his father and brothers to settle in the land of Goshen.
Pharaoh gave the family the best of the land, in Goshen.
The plague of flies spared Goshen, where Israel lived.

identification.modern: Disputed. The Hebrew 'yam suph' is rendered 'Red Sea' or 'Sea of Reeds'; the crossing site is unknown, and proposals include Lake Timsah, the Gulf of Aqaba, the Lake of Tanis, Lake Bardawil and the Ballah Lakes

facts.text: God led Israel by the wilderness road toward the Red Sea.
Israel crossed on dry ground, and the Egyptian army was drowned.
Solomon made a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom.
The Hebrew yam suph, rendered 'Red Sea', literally means 'sea of reeds' and is also used of the Gulf of Aqaba; the exact location of the Exodus crossing is disputed.

identification.modern: Carmel ridge, a coastal mountain range in northern Israel, with Haifa on its northern and western slopes

facts.text: Elijah called Ahab and all Israel to Mount Carmel to decide between the LORD and Baal.
Fire from the LORD fell on Elijah's sacrifice.
The Shunammite woman went to the man of God, Elisha, at Mount Carmel.

identification.modern: Mount Tabor, a hill at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley in Lower Galilee, Israel

facts.text: Barak gathered ten thousand men on Mount Tabor before defeating Sisera.
The Gospels do not name the mountain of the Transfiguration. Matthew says only that Jesus led Peter, James and John up a high mountain.
A tradition links Tabor with the Transfiguration: the earliest identification is by Origen in the 3rd century, later recounted by Cyril of Jerusalem and Jerome in the 4th century.

identification.modern: Traditionally within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in the Old City of Jerusalem; the exact spot is debated

facts.text: Mark says Golgotha means the Place of the Skull.
John says the place of crucifixion was near the city, and that there was a garden with a new tomb nearby.
Since the 4th century Christian tradition has placed Golgotha within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, though the rocky knoll north of the Damascus Gate (Gordon's Calvary) has also been proposed.

identification.modern: Patmos, a Greek island of the Dodecanese in the Aegean Sea, off the west coast of Turkey

facts.text: John writes that he was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.
There he received the vision recorded in the Book of Revelation.

identification.modern: Ruins about 1 km northeast of Yalvaç, Isparta Province, Turkey

facts.text: Paul and Barnabas entered the synagogue here on the Sabbath, and Paul preached.
Paul and Barnabas declared they were turning to the Gentiles after opposition from some of the Jews.
The Jews stirred up leading women and men of the city, started a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district.

identification.modern: The island of Cyprus in the eastern Mediterranean, today divided along a United Nations buffer zone between the Republic of Cyprus and a northern area that calls itself the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, recognised only by Turkey

facts.text: Barnabas, a Levite, was a native of Cyprus.
Barnabas and Saul sailed to Cyprus, preached at Salamis and met the proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos.
After the dispute with Paul, Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus.

identification.modern: Jaffa, the southern part of Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel

facts.text: Peter raised the disciple Tabitha (Dorcas) from the dead at Joppa.
Peter had his vision of the sheet from heaven while staying with Simon the tanner at Joppa.
Jonah went down to Joppa to find a ship to Tarshish.

identification.modern: Caesarea National Park, on the coast of Israel at the western edge of the Sharon plain

facts.text: Cornelius, a Roman centurion at Caesarea, received Peter and was baptized with his household.
Paul was kept prisoner at Caesarea under the governors Felix and Festus.
Herod the Great built a harbour at the old Phoenician settlement and dedicated the town and its port to Caesar Augustus as Caesarea.
